title: hashCode()
summary: Master the hashCode() method: how integer hash codes power O(1) hash tables (HashMap, HashSet), the 31 prime multiplier, and Objects.hash().
learningObjectives: Explain how hash codes map arbitrary objects to 32-bit integer bucket indices
Trace how HashMap and HashSet use hashCode() to achieve average O(1) lookups
Implement custom hashCode() algorithms using the prime 31 multiplier technique
Use java.util.Objects.hash(...) for clean, idiomatic hashing across multiple fields
expectedOutcomes: You can implement efficient, well-distributed hashCode() methods that avoid clustering
You understand the mathematical necessity of the prime number 31 in hash computation

activities.title: Practical Context: Constant-Time Hash Table Lookups

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: Imagine a post office with 100,000 residents. If all incoming mail were thrown into a single colossal pile on the floor, finding a letter for 'Zoe Washington' would require inspecting up to 100,000 letters one by one (O(N) search). Instead, the post office installs 26 sorted wall cubbies labeled A through Z. When a letter arrives, the postal clerk looks at the first letter of the last name: 'W'. They walk straight to bucket 'W' (O(1) bucket jump) and search only the few dozen letters inside that specific bin.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: In Java, `hashCode()` is the function that determines which bucket an object belongs to. `HashMap` uses `hashCode()` to jump directly to the target bucket, then uses `.equals()` to find the exact matching item among any items sharing that bucket.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: `hashCode()` is a fast preliminary filter that narrows down the search space to a single bucket in O(1) time.

activities.content:
When collections store millions of records, searching through an array sequentially in $O(N)$ linear time is too slow.

Hash tables (`HashMap`, `HashSet`) achieve near-instantaneous $O(1)$ constant-time lookups using numeric hash codes to distribute items into buckets.

The `hashCode()` method provides this numerical fingerprint for every Java object.

questions.question: What is the return type of the hashCode() method in Java?
What is the average time complexity of retrieving a value from a HashMap with a well-distributed hashCode()?
questions.explanation: A good hash distribution maps entries evenly across buckets, providing O(1) average lookup time.

questions.question: What happens if every single object returns the constant integer 1 from its hashCode() method?
options: The program crashes with a HashOverflowException
The HashMap still functions logically using equals(), but lookups degrade from O(1) to O(N) due to collisions
The map cannot store more than 1 entry
questions.explanation: Constant hashCode collapses all entries into a single bucket. The map functions via equals(), but lookups become O(N).

questions.question: Why is the prime number 31 traditionally chosen in Java hashCode implementations?
options: It is a prime that distributes bits well and modern JVMs optimize 31 * i to (i << 5) - i
Because 31 is the maximum number of fields in a class
Because Java was created on the 31st of October
It was mandated by the ANSI C standard
questions.explanation: 31 minimizes collision clustering and enables the JIT compiler to replace multiplication with a fast shift-and-subtract.

questions.question: What helper method from java.util.Objects calculates a combined hash code for multiple fields?
questions.explanation: java.util.Objects.hash(Object... values) is the standard utility for generating combined hash codes.

questions.question: Can two completely distinct and unequal objects have the exact same hashCode()?
options: No, hash codes must be strictly unique for every object
Yes, this is known as a hash collision and is mathematically inevitable due to the Pigeonhole Principle
Only if both objects are null
questions.explanation: There are only 2^32 possible int values. Uncountably infinite distinct objects must inevitably collide on the same hash.

questions.question: How should an array field be incorporated into an object's hashCode()?
questions.explanation: Arrays do not override hashCode(). You must call Arrays.hashCode(array) to hash based on array contents.

questions.question: If you don't override hashCode() in your class, what is the default implementation?
options: Returns the length of the class name
Returns the default identity hash code from java.lang.Object
questions.explanation: Default Object.hashCode() derives an integer from the object's internal memory identity.

questions.question: What is the performance overhead of using Objects.hash(f1, f2) compared to manual calculation?
options: Minor overhead due to varargs array allocation and primitive autoboxing
questions.explanation: Objects.hash creates a small temporary varargs Object[] and autoboxes primitives, which is negligible except in extreme performance hotspots.

questions.question: In Java 8+, what data structure does HashMap convert long bucket collision chains into when a bucket exceeds 8 elements?
options: A Red-Black Tree (TreeMap node), improving worst-case search from O(N) to O(log N)
questions.explanation: Java 8+ treeifies collision buckets into Red-Black balanced trees once they exceed 8 elements, guaranteeing O(log N) worst-case lookup.

questions.question: Can you walk through what happens internally inside HashMap.put(key, value)?
questions.answer: 1. It evaluates `key.hashCode()`. 2. It applies a bit-spreading scrambler `(h ^ (h >>> 16))` to prevent poor lower-bit distributions. 3. It calculates bucket index `(n - 1) & hash`. 4. If the bucket is empty, it inserts a new Node. 5. If occupied, it traverses the bucket: if an existing key has matching hash AND `(existingKey == key || key.equals(existingKey))`, it updates the value. Otherwise, it appends a new node (converting to Red-Black tree if bucket size exceeds 8). 6. If table load factor (0.75) is exceeded, it doubles the table capacity and rehashes.

If occupied, it traverses the bucket: if an existing key has matching hash AND `(existingKey == key || key.equals(existingKey))`, it updates the value. Otherwise, it appends a new node (converting to Red-Black tree if bucket size exceeds 8). 6. If table load factor (0.75) is exceeded, it doubles the table capacity and rehashes.
questions.keyTakeaway: HashMap hashes the key, finds the bucket index, verifies with == and equals(), and rehashes when load factor is exceeded.

questions.question: Why must every field used in equals() also be used in hashCode()?
questions.answer: If a field is used in `equals()` but omitted from `hashCode()`, two objects with matching fields might be considered equal by `equals()`, but could end up with different hash codes if another field differs. This violates the golden contract: equal objects MUST have equal hash codes!
questions.expectedAnswer: If a field is used in `equals()` but omitted from `hashCode()`, two objects with matching fields might be considered equal by `equals()`, but could end up with different hash codes if another field differs. This violates the golden contract: equal objects MUST have equal hash codes!
questions.keyTakeaway: Every field that influences equals() MUST be included in hashCode().
keyPoints: Every field that influences equals() MUST be included in hashCode().

questions.question: Is it permissible to exclude fields from hashCode() that ARE in equals()?
questions.answer: NO! You must NEVER exclude an equals-significant field from hashCode. However, it is permissible to exclude fields from both (like cached transient fields or non-significant timestamps).
questions.expectedAnswer: NO! You must NEVER exclude an equals-significant field from hashCode. However, it is permissible to exclude fields from both (like cached transient fields or non-significant timestamps).
questions.keyTakeaway: Equals and hashCode must examine the exact same set of significant fields.
keyPoints: Equals and hashCode must examine the exact same set of significant fields.

questions.question: Can a class cache its hashCode for high-performance immutable objects?
questions.answer: Yes! For immutable objects (like `java.lang.String`), the hash code can be computed once on first use and stored in a private `hash` field. Subsequent calls return the cached integer immediately, achieving zero-cost hashing.
questions.expectedAnswer: Yes! For immutable objects (like `java.lang.String`), the hash code can be computed once on first use and stored in a private `hash` field. Subsequent calls return the cached integer immediately, achieving zero-cost hashing.
questions.keyTakeaway: Immutable objects can lazily compute and cache their hash code for peak performance.
keyPoints: Immutable objects can lazily compute and cache their hash code for peak performance.

questions.question: What is the HashDOS vulnerability and how did Java 8 fix it?
questions.answer: Attackers can craft thousands of malicious keys that all produce the exact same hashCode, causing massive bucket collisions and degrading server response times from O(1) to O(N^2) (denial of service). Java 8 fixed this by converting collision buckets into balanced Red-Black trees (O(log N)) when bucket depth exceeds 8.
questions.expectedAnswer: Attackers can craft thousands of malicious keys that all produce the exact same hashCode, causing massive bucket collisions and degrading server response times from O(1) to O(N^2) (denial of service). Java 8 fixed this by converting collision buckets into balanced Red-Black trees (O(log N)) when bucket depth exceeds 8.
questions.keyTakeaway: Treeification in Java 8 protects HashMaps against HashDOS collision attacks.
keyPoints: Treeification in Java 8 protects HashMaps against HashDOS collision attacks.

questions.question: How do you hash primitive boolean, float, and double types manually in Java?
questions.answer: For `boolean`, use `(b ? 1231 : 1237)`. For `float`, use `Float.floatToIntBits(f)`. For `double`, use `Double.doubleToLongBits(d)`, then fold the 64-bit long into 32-bit int: `(int)(bits ^ (bits >>> 32))`.
questions.expectedAnswer: For `boolean`, use `(b ? 1231 : 1237)`. For `float`, use `Float.floatToIntBits(f)`. For `double`, use `Double.doubleToLongBits(d)`, then fold the 64-bit long into 32-bit int: `(int)(bits ^ (bits >>> 32))`.
questions.keyTakeaway: Use Float.floatToIntBits and Double.doubleToLongBits to fold floating-point values into hash codes.
keyPoints: Use Float.floatToIntBits and Double.doubleToLongBits to fold floating-point values into hash codes.

practiceProblems.title: Stock Ticker hashCode() Implementation
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `hashCode()` in `StockTicker` using `java.util.Objects.hash(symbol, exchange)`. Also implement `equals(Object obj)`. Verify that two instances with the same symbol and exchange produce identical hash codes.
hints: Implement equals using Objects.equals on symbol and exchange.

practiceProblems.title: Manual Prime 31 Hashing for GeoBoundingBox
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a `GeoBoundingBox` class with a manual prime 31 hash implementation from scratch:
1. Class `GeoBoundingBox`: holds `private int minLat`, `private int maxLat`, `private int minLon`, `private int maxLon`.
   - Constructor initializes all four.
   - Override `equals(Object obj)`: all four integers must match.
   - Override `hashCode()` using the manual prime 31 recipe:
     - `int result = 17;`
     - `result = 31 * result + minLat;`
     - `result = 31 * result + maxLat;`
     - `result = 31 * result + minLon;`
     - `result = 31 * result + maxLon;`
     - `return result;`
2. In `Main`, create box1 = new GeoBoundingBox(10, 20, 30, 40) and box2 = new GeoBoundingBox(10, 20, 30, 40).
3. Print `'Equal: ' + box1.equals(box2)`.
4. Print `'Hashes match: ' + (box1.hashCode() == box2.hashCode())`.
hints: Accumulate hash into result using `result = 31 * result + field;`.

practiceProblems.title: Lazy Caching of Hash Code for Immutable Token
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build an immutable security token with lazy hash caching from scratch:
1. Class `CryptoToken`: holds `private final String rawHex` and `private int cachedHash = 0` (mutable cache field!).
   - Constructor initializes `rawHex`.
   - Override `equals(Object obj)`: matches if rawHex matches.
   - Override `hashCode()` with lazy caching:
     - If `cachedHash == 0`, compute `cachedHash = rawHex.hashCode();`.
     - Return `cachedHash;`.
   - Method `public boolean isHashCached()` returns `cachedHash != 0`.
2. In `Main`, create token = new CryptoToken("9f8a3b2c").
3. Print `'Hash cached before call: ' + token.isHashCached()` (false).
4. Call `token.hashCode()`.
5. Print `'Hash cached after call: ' + token.isHashCached()` (true).
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Hash cached before call: false
Hash cached after call: true
hints: Check cachedHash == 0, compute on demand, and save to cachedHash.
Subsequent calls return cachedHash instantly without recalculation.

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Forgetting to Hash Array Contents
practiceProblems.problemStatement: A developer wrote a `ByteSignature` class containing a `byte[] data` array. But in `hashCode()`, they wrote `return Objects.hash(data);`, which hashes the array's memory address pointer instead of its byte values! Fix `hashCode()` to use `java.util.Arrays.hashCode(data)` and `equals()` to use `java.util.Arrays.equals(data, other.data)`.

practiceProblems.title: Hash Table Bucket Distribution Simulator
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Simulate a hash bucket distribution engine from scratch:
1. Class `SimpleBucketTable`:
   - Holds `private int bucketCount` (e.g. 10).
   - Holds `private int[] bucketSizes` initialized to size `bucketCount`.
   - Constructor accepts `int bucketCount`.
   - Method `public void insert(Object item)`:
     - Computes index: `int idx = Math.abs(item.hashCode()) % bucketCount;`.
     - Increments `bucketSizes[idx]++`.
   - Method `public void printDistribution()`: prints `'=== Bucket Histogram ==='` and for each bucket `0` to `bucketCount - 1` prints `'Bucket ' + i + ': ' + bucketSizes[i] + ' items'`.
2. In `Main`, create a table with 4 buckets. Insert 8 String items: 'Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry', 'Date', 'Elderberry', 'Fig', 'Grape', 'Honeydew'. Call `printDistribution()`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
=== Bucket Histogram ===
Bucket 0: 3 items
Bucket 1: 0 items
Bucket 2: 2 items
Bucket 3: 3 items
hints: Verify the distribution counts for the standard JDK String hash codes.
